unitKey: 2Solid, liquid, gas states and changes of stateChemistry

questions.question: If pure water is heated until it boils at 100°C, at what temperature will the resulting steam begin to condense back into liquid water if it is cooled under the same atmospheric pressure?
A closed, flexible container holds 10 ml of liquid water. If this water is completely boiled into steam, what happens to the volume of the container?
options: It decreases significantly because gas particles are smaller.
It increases significantly because the substance expands in the gas state.
It remains exactly the same because the mass of water has not changed.
It increases slightly by about 10% because of thermal expansion of the liquid.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the behavior of water particles as steam cools and condenses into liquid water?
options: The particles stop moving entirely and lock into fixed positions.
The particles move further apart and gain kinetic energy.
The particles move closer together as they transition to the liquid state.
The individual particles shrink in size to occupy less space.

questions.question: A student notices that their Bunsen burner is producing a yellow, sooty flame that is leaving black marks on a beaker. How can they adjust the burner to get a hotter, cleaner flame?
options: Close the air hole completely to restrict the oxygen flow.
Open the air hole to allow more air to mix with the gas.
Turn the gas tap down to reduce the gas flow.
Turn the gas tap up to increase the gas pressure.

questions.question: What is the safest way to carry a lit wooden splint across a science laboratory to light a Bunsen burner?
options: Hold it vertically upwards to keep the flame away from your hand.
Hold it horizontally and walk as quickly as possible to prevent it from going out.
Hold it with the flame angled slightly downwards, shielding the flame with your other hand.
Hold it angled upwards at 45 degrees, blowing gently on it to keep it lit.

questions.question: Equal masses of a substance exist in solid, liquid, and gas states. Which state has the highest amount of energy, and which has the lowest?
options: Gas state has the most energy; solid state has the least energy.
Solid state has the most energy; gas state has the least energy.
Liquid state has the most energy; solid state has the least energy.
Gas state has the most energy; liquid state has the least energy.

questions.question: A puddle of water on a playground disappears after a few hours on a cool day when the temperature is only 15°C. Why does this happen?
options: Water can only transition to a gas when it reaches its boiling point of 100°C, so the water must have soaked entirely into the ground.
Liquid water can evaporate into a gas at temperatures well below its boiling point.
The sun must have heated the puddle to exactly 100°C locally for a fraction of a second.
The air pressure must have dropped to zero to allow the water to boil at 15°C.

questions.question: Two identical dishes contain equal amounts of water. Dish A is kept at 20°C, and Dish B is kept at 40°C. Which dish will dry out first, and why?
options: Dish A, because cooler water particles are more tightly packed and push each other out.
Dish B, because hotter water evaporates more quickly.
Both dishes will dry out at the exact same rate because evaporation is independent of temperature.
Dish B, because the water in Dish B has reached its boiling point.

questions.question: Wet laundry is hung outside on a cloudy day when the temperature is 12°C. Which statement is correct regarding the drying of the clothes?
options: The clothes will not dry because water requires a temperature of 100°C to evaporate.
The clothes will dry because water evaporates at temperatures lower than 100°C.
The clothes will only dry if the air temperature rises to at least 50°C.
The clothes will dry because the water freezes and then falls off as ice.

questions.question: A pure sample of a metal is found to melt at exactly 660°C. At what temperature will this liquid metal begin to freeze back into a solid?
Why does a solid block of iron maintain a fixed shape and refuse to flow when placed into a large bowl?
options: The particles are free to move around each other, but they are extremely heavy.
The forces of attraction between the particles hold them in fixed positions.
There are no forces of attraction, but the particles are packed so tightly they cannot move.
The particles are constantly expanding and contracting to fill the volume.

questions.question: When water is poured from a beaker into a graduated cylinder, it changes its shape to match the cylinder but does not expand to fill the entire room. What does this tell us about the particles in a liquid?
options: They are held in rigid, fixed positions but can rotate slightly.
They have completely overcome all forces of attraction and move independently.
They are held together but have enough energy to break free and move around each other.
They have no forces of attraction between them but are held down by gravity alone.

questions.question: Substance X melts at -182°C, while Substance Y melts at 1538°C. What can you infer about the forces of attraction between the particles in these two substances?
options: The forces of attraction between particles in Substance X are much stronger than in Substance Y.
The forces of attraction between particles in Substance Y are much stronger than in Substance X.
Both substances have identical forces of attraction, but Substance Y has larger particles.
Substance X has no forces of attraction, while Substance Y has only gravitational attraction.

questions.question: A thermometer is placed in a beaker of melting ice, then held in a room, and finally held in a healthy human's hand. What sequence of temperatures would you expect to read?
options: 0°C, then about 20°C, then about 37°C
0°C, then about 37°C, then about 20°C
100°C, then about 20°C, then about 37°C
-10°C, then about 25°C, then about 98°C

questions.question: Why can a large volume of air inside a bicycle pump be easily squeezed into a much smaller volume, whereas water inside a syringe cannot?
options: Water particles are much harder than air particles.
In the gas state, a substance can be compressed because there are large gaps between particles, unlike in the liquid state.
Air particles are constantly shrinking when pressure is applied.
Liquid water has stronger magnetic forces that push back against the syringe.

questions.question: Why do gas particles spread out to completely fill any container they are placed in, rather than settling at the bottom like a liquid?
options: Gas particles have enough energy to be free of the attractive forces between them.
Gas particles are lighter than gravity, so they float upwards.
Gas particles are repelled by the bottom of the container.
The forces of attraction between gas particles actually push them away from each other.

questions.question: If you could zoom in to look at the space between the nitrogen and oxygen particles in clean, dry air, what would you find in those gaps?
options: Tiny particles of water vapor and dust.
Nothing at all (a vacuum).
A thin, weightless fluid that carries heat.
Compressed liquid air.

questions.question: The melting point of gallium is 29.76°C. If a sample of gallium is kept in a freezer at -10°C, what state of matter will it be in?
options: Liquid state
Solid state
Gas state
A mixture of liquid and gas states

questions.question: The freezing point of mercury is -38.83°C, and its boiling point is 356.7°C. If a sample of mercury is at 20°C, what state of matter is it in?
options: Solid state
Gas state
Liquid state
It is transitioning from gas to solid

questions.question: When steam inside a sealed, flexible balloon cools down and condenses back into liquid water, what happens to the volume occupied by the water substance?
options: The volume increases because liquid particles take up more space than gas particles.
The volume decreases because the substance occupies less space in its liquid state.
The volume remains unchanged because the number of particles is the same.
The volume increases slightly because of the expansion of liquid water.

questions.question: If pure water is being cooled from 120°C, at what temperature will it transition from a gas to a liquid, and what is this temperature point called?
options: 100°C, its condensing point
100°C, its melting point
0°C, its freezing point
120°C, its boiling point

questions.question: During an experiment, a student boils liquid nitrogen to form nitrogen gas. Which statement best describes what happens to the nitrogen particles during this state change?
options: The particles grow in size to occupy the new volume.
The particles move much further apart from each other.
The particles begin to vibrate in fixed positions.
The particles lose energy and clump together

questions.question: A student wants to heat a beaker of water as quickly as possible without leaving soot on the bottom of the beaker. What adjustment should they make to the Bunsen burner, and why?
options: Close the air hole completely to get a bright yellow-orange flame.
Open the air hole to get a hotter, cleaner blue flame.
Turn down the gas tap to make the orange flame smaller.
Remove the collar completely so that the air cannot mix with the gas.

questions.question: When moving across a laboratory to light a Bunsen burner with a wooden splint, what is the safest way to carry the lit splint?
options: Pointing vertically upwards to keep the flame away from the floor.
Angled slightly downwards and shielded with your other hand.
Held horizontally at arm's length while walking quickly.
Waving it gently from side to side so it does not extinguish.

questions.question: Equal masses of the same substance are compared in its solid, liquid, and gas states. Which of the following correctly ranks the states from the one with the least total energy to the one with the most total energy?
options: Gas, liquid, solid
Solid, liquid, gas
Liquid, solid, gas
Gas, solid, liquid

questions.question: A puddle of water on a pavement disappears on a cool autumn day when the temperature is only 12°C. How is this possible?
options: Water can only change to a gas when it reaches its boiling point of 100°C.
Water in its liquid state can evaporate at temperatures well below its boiling point.
The water must have sunk into the solid concrete rather than turning into gas.
The cold air forced the water to freeze and then immediately sublimate.

questions.question: An industrial dryer needs to remove moisture from fabric. Based on the behavior of water, why is hot air used instead of cold air?
options: Hot water evaporates more slowly, allowing the fabric to dry more evenly.
Hot air increases the boiling point of the water so it can boil instantly.
The hotter the water, the more quickly it evaporates.
Hot air chemically converts water particles into hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.question: A sample of a pure unknown metal is observed to melt at exactly 660°C. If you have a liquid sample of this same pure metal and cool it down, at what temperature will it begin to freeze?
options: At a temperature much lower than 660°C, because freezing requires much less energy.
At exactly 660°C, because the melting point and freezing point of a pure substance are the same.
At 0°C, because all liquids freeze at the same temperature as water.
At a temperature higher than 660°C, because liquid particles have more energy.

questions.question: Why does a solid iron bar maintain its fixed shape and refuse to flow when placed into a large bucket?
options: The particles in a solid are held in fixed positions by forces of attraction between them.
The particles are extremely large and cannot squeeze past each other.
There is absolutely no energy remaining in the particles of a solid.
The forces of attraction between the particles have been completely broken.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why liquid water can flow and take the shape of its container, yet cannot easily be compressed into a smaller volume?
options: The particles have no forces of attraction between them, allowing them to move completely independently.
The particles are held together but have enough energy to break free and move around each other.
The particles are fixed in a rigid grid but vibrate very violently.
The particles are separated by massive gaps filled with air.

questions.question: Substance X melts at -97°C, while Substance Y melts at 801°C. What does this tell us about the forces of attraction between the particles in these two substances?
options: Substance X has stronger forces of attraction between its particles than Substance Y.
Substance Y has stronger forces of attraction between its particles than Substance X.
Both substances have identical forces of attraction, but Substance Y is much heavier.
Neither substance has any forces of attraction between its particles when solid.

questions.question: If you place a beaker of pure water in a room kept at exactly 20°C, what state will the water be in, and what is this temperature commonly referred to?
options: Solid state, because 20°C is below the freezing point of water.
Liquid state, because 20°C is room temperature, which is above the freezing point of water.
Gas state, because 20°C is body temperature, which causes rapid boiling.
Liquid state, because 20°C is the boiling point of water.

questions.question: A scientist pumps a small amount of gas into a large, sealed, empty glass jar. Which of the following correctly describes the behavior of the gas?
options: It sinks to the bottom of the jar and maintains a flat, fixed surface.
It clumps together in the center of the jar in a fixed solid shape.
It flows to fill the entire container and can be compressed if the jar's volume is reduced.
It cannot flow or be compressed because gases behave exactly like liquids.

questions.question: Why is a gas able to expand indefinitely to fill any container it is placed in?
options: The particles have enough energy to be free of the attractive forces between them.
The particles are constantly dividing to create more particles.
The forces of attraction between gas particles become infinitely strong.
Air pressure outside the container actively pulls the gas particles apart.

questions.question: If you could zoom in and look at a sample of pure helium gas, what would you find in the spaces between the helium particles?
options: Tiny particles of air and water vapor
Pure liquid helium filling the gaps
Nothing at all
Heat energy in the form of a light blue liquid

questions.question: A heavy copper block is moved from a small wooden crate into a large spherical glass bowl. How do the shape and volume of the copper block change?
options: It flows to take the shape of the bowl, but its volume remains the same.
It maintains its fixed shape, does not flow, and cannot be compressed.
It expands to fill the entire bowl and can easily be compressed.
It crumbles into a liquid-like state because its container has changed.

questions.question: If 50 ml of liquid water is poured from a tall narrow cylinder into a wide flat dish, what happens to the water?
options: It keeps its original cylinder shape and refuses to spread out.
It flows to take the shape of the dish, but its volume cannot be compressed to a smaller size.
It instantly compresses itself to occupy only half of its original volume.
It expands to fill the entire room as a gas.

questions.question: A student looks at a clear, pure sample of liquid alcohol under a standard classroom school microscope but cannot see any individual particles. Why is this?
options: Liquid alcohol does not contain any particles until it freezes.
The particles have melted and merged into one continuous giant particle.
All substances are made of particles that are far too small to see with the naked eye or standard microscopes.
Alcohol is a gas in disguise and has no physical particles.

questions.question: When a kettle of water boils on a stove, the lid starts to rattle and lift. What physical change causes this effect?
options: The water particles shrink, leaving more empty space that pushes the lid.
The substance increases significantly in volume when it transitions to the gas state.
The liquid water expands slightly as it turns into ice inside the kettle.
The metal of the kettle contracts, forcing the water level to rise.

questions.question: If a sealed, flexible bag filled with hot water vapor is cooled down until the vapor condenses back into liquid water, what will happen to the volume of the bag?
options: The volume will decrease because a substance decreases in volume when it condenses into a liquid.
The volume will increase because liquid particles are much larger than gas particles.
The volume will remain exactly the same because the mass of the water has not changed.
The volume will expand violently because condensing releases trapped air.

questions.question: If pure water is heated until it boils, and the steam produced is captured and cooled until it condenses, how do the boiling point and condensing point of this water compare?
options: The boiling point is 100°C, but the condensing point is slightly lower due to energy loss.
The boiling point is 100°C, which is exactly the same temperature as its condensing point.
The boiling point is higher than 100°C, while the condensing point is lower than 100°C.
The condensing point is 100°C, but the boiling point can vary depending on the heating rate.

questions.question: When 10 ml of liquid water is completely boiled in a sealed, flexible container, what happens to the total volume occupied by the water substance?
options: It remains exactly 10 ml because the mass of the water has not changed.
It decreases because gas particles are smaller than liquid particles.
It increases significantly because the substance increases in volume in the gas state.
It increases slightly only because the temperature of the container increases.

questions.question: During a laboratory experiment, steam is cooled inside a syringe until it condenses into liquid water. What happens to the water particles during this condensation process?
options: The particles move closer together.
The particles shrink in size.
The particles stop moving completely.
The particles move further apart.

questions.question: A student is heating a beaker of water and notices black soot forming on the bottom of the beaker. What adjustment should they make to the Bunsen burner to prevent this and heat the water faster?
options: Close the air hole to make the flame orange and quieter.
Open the air hole to change the flame to a hotter, cleaner, blue flame.
Turn the gas tap down to reduce the supply of gas to the burner.
Blow gently on the flame to increase the oxygen supply.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the correct and safe way to transport a lit wooden splint across a science laboratory to light a Bunsen burner?
options: Hold the splint pointing vertically upwards to prevent it from burning down too quickly.
Run quickly with the splint held horizontally so the flame does not blow out.
Carry the splint with the flame angled slightly downwards and shielded by the other hand.
Hold the splint pointing directly downwards with your arm fully extended to your side.

questions.question: An equal mass of a substance is kept at three different temperatures so that it exists as a solid, a liquid, and a gas. How does the energy of the substance compare across these three states?
options: The solid state has the most energy, and the gas state has the least.
The liquid state has the most energy, while the solid and gas states have equal energy.
The gas state has the most energy, and the solid state has the least.
All three states have the same amount of energy because the mass is equal.

questions.question: A shallow puddle of water on a road disappears after a few hours on a cool autumn day when the temperature is only 12°C. Which statement best explains this?
options: Liquid water can only turn into a gas when it reaches its boiling point of 100°C.
The water must have soaked entirely into the road because evaporation cannot occur below 100°C.
A substance in its liquid state can evaporate at temperatures below its boiling point.
The air temperature of 12°C is actually above the boiling point of impure rainwater.

questions.question: Two identical cups, one containing hot water at 80°C and the other containing cold water at 20°C, are left in the same room. Why does the level of water in the hot cup decrease faster?
options: The hotter the water, the more quickly it evaporates.
Cold water cannot evaporate at room temperature, so its level remains completely constant.
The hot water is boiling, which is the only way water can escape into the air.
The cold water is absorbing moisture from the air, which refills the cup.

questions.question: A scientist measures the temperature of a drying puddle of pure water and finds it is 15°C. Is it possible for water to evaporate at this temperature?
options: No, because evaporation is another word for boiling, which only happens at 100°C.
Yes, because water evaporates at temperatures that are lower than 100°C.
No, because water only evaporates when the air temperature is at least 50°C.
Yes, but only if the water is boiling rapidly at 15°C.

questions.question: When liquid candle wax is left to cool, it gradually hardens into solid wax. Which of the following describes this change of state?
options: Melting, where a liquid changes to a solid.
When it freezes, a substance changes from the liquid state to the solid state.
Condensation, where a gas changes to a solid.
Evaporation, where a liquid changes to a gas.

questions.question: A sample of pure chemical X melts at 45°C. What is the freezing point of this same pure chemical X?
options: 0°C, because all substances freeze at the same temperature as water.
90°C, which is double the melting point.
45°C, because the melting point and freezing point of a pure substance are the same temperature.
-45°C, because freezing is the negative opposite of melting.

questions.question: Why does a solid iron block maintain a fixed shape and not flow when transferred from a small box to a larger tray?
options: The particles are free to slide past each other but cannot escape.
The particles have high kinetic energy and repel each other into fixed positions.
In the solid state, forces of attraction between particles hold them in fixed positions.
There are no forces of attraction, leaving the particles stuck in place by gravity.

questions.question: How do the forces and movement of particles in liquid water compare to those in solid ice?
options: Particles in liquid water have no forces of attraction between them at all.
Particles in liquid water are held in fixed positions but vibrate much faster than in ice.
In the liquid state, particles are held together but have enough energy to break free to move around.
Particles in liquid water are further apart than in steam and cannot move.

questions.question: Substance A melts at -100°C, while Substance B melts at 1500°C. What can you infer about the forces of attraction between the particles in these two substances?
options: The forces of attraction between particles in Substance A are much stronger than in Substance B.
The stronger the force of attraction between particles in a substance, the higher its melting point, so B has stronger forces.
Both substances have identical forces of attraction, but Substance B has larger particles.
Substance A has no forces of attraction, while Substance B has repulsive forces.

questions.question: A beaker of water is kept in a room at 20°C. A student places their finger into the water. What are the correct temperatures of freezing water, the room, and the student's body?
options: Water freezes at 100°C, room temperature is 37°C, and body temperature is 20°C.
Water freezes at 0°C, room temperature is about 20°C, and body temperature is about 37°C.
Water freezes at 0°C, room temperature is 37°C, and body temperature is 100°C.
Water freezes at -10°C, room temperature is 20°C, and body temperature is 98°C.

questions.question: A gas is pumped into a syringe, and the plunger is pushed down. The gas flows to fill the new shape, shrinks in volume, and fills the entire container. Which properties of a gas does this demonstrate?
options: In the gas state a substance has a fixed shape, cannot flow, and can be compressed.
In the gas state a substance can flow, it fills the whole of a container and can be compressed.
In the gas state a substance cannot flow, does not fill its container, and cannot be compressed.
In the gas state a substance can flow, has a fixed volume, and cannot be compressed.

questions.question: Why are gas particles able to spread out and fill any size container they are placed in?
options: In the gas state, particles have enough energy to be free of the attractive forces between them.
The particles are extremely large and physically crowd each other out.
Gravity pulls gas particles upwards, overcoming all other forces.
The attractive forces between gas particles are stronger than in solids, pulling them apart.

questions.question: If we could look at a container of pure helium gas under an imaginary super-microscope, what would we find in the space between the helium atoms?
options: Air molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen.
Tiny particles of heat energy.
Liquid helium filling the gaps.
There is nothing at all between the particles.

questions.question: A heavy granite block is placed inside a round bowl. The granite does not change its shape to match the bowl, does not flow, and its volume cannot be reduced by pressing on it. What state of matter properties does this show?
options: In the solid state a substance can flow, fills the container, and can be compressed.
In the solid state a substance has a fixed shape, it does not flow and cannot be compressed.
In the solid state a substance has a fixed shape, can flow, and can be compressed.
In the solid state a substance has a flexible shape, flows slowly, and can be compressed.

questions.question: When juice is poured from a carton into a glass, it flows easily and takes the shape of the glass, but you cannot squeeze the glass to make the juice occupy a smaller volume. What state of matter properties are described?
options: In the liquid state a substance can flow, fills the container, and can be compressed.
In the liquid state a substance has a fixed shape, cannot flow, and can be compressed.
In the liquid state a substance can flow, it fills the shape of its container and cannot be compressed.
In the liquid state a substance cannot flow, has a fixed shape, and can be compressed.
